title: A study to see how best to treat ear discharge in children
official: Management of acute Ear Discharge in Children (MEDIC): a feasibility study
summary:
Background and study aims  
This study looks at the best way to treat ear infections in children when fluid leaks from the ear. This condition is called acute otitis media with discharge. It happens when an infected eardrum bursts and liquid drains out. The study aims to compare two treatments: oral antibiotics and antibiotic ear drops. Researchers want to find out if it is possible to run a larger study in the future and whether parents can use a remote online consent process.

Who can participate?  
Children aged 6 months to under 7 years can take part if they have a new episode of ear discharge lasting less than 6 weeks. They must not have had antibiotics recently. Children cannot take part if they have serious illness, complications of ear infections, certain medical conditions of the ear, or allergies to the study medicines.

What does the study involve?
Children will be chosen at random to receive either oral antibiotics or antibiotic ear drops for 7 days. Parents will be contacted by the study team through phone calls and text messages to check how their child is doing and whether the ear discharge has stopped. The design aims to fit around busy family life.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?  
Children may benefit from treatment that helps clear their ear infection. The study may also help improve care for future families. Risks include possible side effects from antibiotics, such as stomach upset from oral medicines. Ear drops carry very little risk because they are absorbed into the body at low levels. If any problems occur, families can contact the study team.

Where is the study run from?  
The study is run from Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, with clinical work based at Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?  
December 2026 to September 2027

Who is funding the study?  
National Institute for Health and Care Research (UK).

Who is the main contact?  
Mr Elliot Heward at the Paediatric ENT research office, Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital, e.heward@nhs.net
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Current key inclusion criteria:
1.  Children and young people aged ≥6 months and <7 years
2.  Unilateral or bilateral otorrhoea
3.  New episode of otorrhoea (>6 weeks from previous episode)
4.  Otorrhoea duration <6 weeks
5.  No prior antibiotic treatment for this episode
6.  No antibiotics for other reasons within 6 weeks prior
7. Parent/guardian who can understand written English, Urdu, Arabic, Punjabi or Polish




Previous key inclusion criteria:
1.  Children and young people aged ≥6 months and <7 years
2.  Unilateral or bilateral otorrhoea
3.  New episode of otorrhoea (>6 weeks from previous episode)
4.  Otorrhoea duration <6 weeks
5.  No prior antibiotic treatment for this episode
6.  No antibiotics for other reasons within 6 weeks prior
7. Parent/guardian who is able to understand written English, Urdu, Arabic, Punjabi or Polish
Exclusion criteria:
Current key exclusion criteria:
1.  Signs of sepsis (requiring hospitalisation)
2.  Complications of ear infections (e.g. mastoiditis, facial nerve palsy, brain abscess, meningitis)
3.  Significant immunosuppression
4.  Known grommet in the affected ear
5.  Known cholesteatoma in the affected ear
6.  Hypersensitivity to ciprofloxacin *or any member of the quinolone class of antimicrobial agents*
7.  Hypersensitivity to amoxicillin *or to any of the penicillins, or history of a severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction to another betalactam agent (e.g. a cephalosporin, carbapenem or monobactam)* and any contraindication to clarithromycin as per section 4.3 of the SmPC (not just allergy)
8. Currently participating in an ear related research study
9. Currently involved or have been involved with a trial which involves antibiotic treatment within the prior 6 weeks




Previous key exclusion criteria:
1.  Signs of sepsis (requiring hospitalisation)
2.  Complications of ear infections (for example mastoiditis, facial nerve palsy, brain abscess, meningitis)
3.  Significant immunosuppression
4.  Known grommet in the affected ear
5.  Known cholesteatoma in the affected ear
6.  Allergy to ciprofloxacin
7.  Allergy to both amoxicillin and clarithromycin
8. Currently participating in an ear related research study
